_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 14:35:25Z)**_

Yes on both — you've got it exactly.

**Learning from failures.** Right now, when a multi-step operation fails partway and rolls back, the record of what happened is deleted. The proposal is to keep those.

Concretely: a customer checks out. Payment captures fine, then the inventory reservation fails. The workflow compensates — releases what it reserved, voids the payment. Today the merchant sees an order that didn't complete and has **no way to find out why**. The execution record existed for a moment and was deleted precisely because the workflow finished (`FAILED` counts as finished).

After the change, they'd open that run and see: step 1 succeeded, step 2 succeeded, step 3 failed with this error, steps 2 and 1 compensated — plus the exact input the workflow ran with.

**Dropping the successful ones.** Yes, and that's the part that makes it defensible. Successful runs are high-volume and low-value — nobody debugs a checkout that worked. Failures are rare and high-value. Keeping only failures gets you most of the benefit for a small fraction of the storage, which answers the obvious "won't this bloat the database" objection before a reviewer raises it.

## On the UI

**The UI already exists. It ships with Medusa today.** Nobody downloads anything.

Medusa is self-hosted — a merchant installs it and gets the admin dashboard, exactly like your `:9000/app`. That dashboard already contains a workflow inspector at `/app/settings/workflows`:

```
workflow-execution-list/          table of every run
workflow-execution-detail/
  ├── general-section
  ├── timeline-section       <- which steps ran, which compensated
  ├── history-section
  └── payload-section        <- the input it ran with
```

Real, built, functional. You saw it — it rendered fine, it just had nothing in it. That's not a broken page; it's a page with no rows to display, because the rows were deleted.

**So the change isn't building UI. It's making the data exist that the existing UI was built to show.** That's what makes a Large-scoped proposal unusually achievable — the expensive half is already done, and it's sitting unused.

A useful way to frame it in the issue: Medusa built a debugging tool, then made it invisible by default. The feature is turning it on for the cases that matter.

**Who benefits** — worth being precise, since D2 asks who:

- **Merchants/operators** — can see why an order half-completed instead of filing a support ticket
- **Developers** — can debug a custom workflow's compensation logic without adding logging

Not end shoppers; they never see the admin dashboard.

One thing worth doing before you file: **complete a checkout in your storefront.** `complete-cart` is the one workflow that retains, so that would put a real row in the table and let you see a populated timeline. Proposing a change to a page you've actually seen working is much stronger if anyone asks you about it.

Want me to help drive that checkout, or search upstream Medusa first to check nobody's already proposed this?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 14:39:10Z)**_

**Go look at it now:**

```
http://localhost:9000/app/settings/workflows
```

There's one row: `complete-cart`, state `done`, `retention_time` 259200 seconds — exactly the `THREE_DAYS` from `complete-cart.ts:340`. The one workflow in 339 that opts in.

Order created: `order_01M2NAFW4E0KVMYCX91DWSNV7M`, 20 EUR, Medusa Shorts. It'll also show in the Orders list, which was empty in your screenshot.

Click into the execution and look at the **timeline** — this is what the proposal is about. That single checkout ran a deeply nested step tree:

```
acquire-lock-step
  cart-query
    validate-cart-items
      validate-cart-payments
        compensate-payment-if-needed        <- compensation is built in
          validate
            shipping-options-query
              validate-shipping
                create-orders
                  reserve-inventory-step
                  authorize-payment-session-step
                  add-order-transaction
                  create-order
                  release-lock-step
```

Note `compensate-payment-if-needed` — the rollback path is a first-class step, not an afterthought. And `reserve-inventory-step` sits right before `authorize-payment-session-step`, which is exactly the failure scenario we discussed: inventory reserved, then payment fails, and the reservation has to be released.

**Now the argument makes itself.** You're looking at a `done` execution, which is the *least* useful kind — the checkout worked, nobody needs to debug it. Yet it's the only kind you can see, because `complete-cart` is the only workflow that opted in.

Every other workflow — order fulfillment, refunds, returns, inventory adjustments, all 338 of them — produces this same detailed tree, and **throws it away**, including when it fails and compensates. The exact tree you're looking at is what a merchant would need after a half-completed order, and it would not exist.

That's your issue, and now you've seen the page populated rather than taking my word for it.

Worth noting for your writeup: `retention_time` is stored per-execution as an integer (seconds), so the data model already supports per-workflow policy. The feature is about defaults and configuration, not schema — which strengthens the "expensive half is already built" framing.

Want me to search upstream Medusa for prior discussion of this, then draft the issue?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 14:41:46Z)**_

Good question — this is the core mental model, and it's worth getting exactly right.

**Workflows are definitions written in code. Executions are runs of them.** Like a class and its instances, or a recipe and each time you cook it.

- `complete-cart` is **one** workflow, written once in `packages/core/core-flows/src/cart/workflows/complete-cart.ts`. It ships with Medusa.
- Every checkout creates a **new execution** of that same definition.
- The 339 count is *definitions*. Executions are unbounded.

So to answer directly:

| | |
|---|---|
| Created in advance | The **workflow definitions** — 339 of them, written by Medusa's developers, shipped in the codebase |
| Created per order | The **execution** — a new run, with its own transaction id, step states, and payload |

Nothing generates a new workflow per order. Placing an order runs the same `complete-cart` code that every other order runs. What's unique per order is the *record of that run*.

Two clarifications on top:

**You can write your own workflows.** That's the "Framework" half of Medusa — `createWorkflow()` and `createStep()` are public API. A store with unusual requirements defines custom workflows alongside the 339 built-in ones. Those are also definitions written in advance.

**Workflows aren't only for orders.** All 339 cover fulfillment, refunds, returns, inventory adjustments, product imports, customer operations — any multi-step operation that needs rollback.

**Which brings the proposal into focus.** You asked whether we want to catch failures in an existing workflow or in creating a new one — it's the first, and there is no second. We want failed **executions** of existing definitions retained.

Right now you're looking at two `done` executions, which is the useless case. If order #3's inventory reservation had failed and rolled back, that execution would have been written and then **deleted**, because `FAILED` counts as finished. The one run worth keeping is the one guaranteed to disappear.

You could actually demonstrate this — force a failure by ordering more units than exist in stock, then check whether a row appears. That'd be strong evidence for the issue, and it'd take a few minutes. Want me to?

TITLE: Retain failed and reverted workflow executions so the admin timeline can display them

LABELS: type: improvement, scope: large

---

**Summary**

Medusa runs business logic as workflows: multi step operations where each step can declare a
compensation function that undoes it if a later step fails. The admin dashboard includes a
workflow execution viewer at `/app/settings/workflows` with a list view and a detail view
containing general, timeline, history, and payload sections.

That viewer is already built to display failures. `constants.ts` defines
`STEP_ERROR_STATES` as `[FAILED, REVERTED, TIMEOUT, DORMANT]` and `STEP_SKIPPED_STATES` as
`[SKIPPED, SKIPPED_FAILURE]`, and the timeline component colors each step from those lists
at `workflow-execution-timeline-section.tsx:416-425`, rendering failed steps red and
compensating steps orange. `utils.ts:44-50` has translated labels for `failed`, `reverted`,
and `waiting_to_compensate`.

The problem is that the data those code paths need is deleted before anyone can see it.
A workflow execution is only persisted if the workflow sets `retentionTime`. Out of 339
`createWorkflow()` calls in `core-flows`, exactly one sets it: `complete-cart.ts:340`, at
three days. Every other execution is removed when the run finishes.

"Finished" includes failure. In
`workflow-engine-inmemory/src/utils/workflow-orchestrator-storage.ts`, `finishedStates` is
`[DONE, FAILED, REVERTED]` (lines 43 to 47), and at line 415 a finished run without
`retentionTime` is passed to `deleteFromDb`. The Redis engine does the same at line 631, so
this is a platform wide policy rather than a single engine bug.

The result is that a workflow which failed and rolled back is discarded at exactly the
moment its record becomes useful. A merchant whose order half completed has no structured
record of which step failed, what compensated, or what input the run received, even though
the dashboard contains a viewer designed to show precisely that.

Verified locally on Medusa 2.17.2. After completing two checkouts through the Store API,
`workflow_execution` contained two `complete-cart` rows in state `done`, which are the least
useful executions to keep. No other workflow produced a row.

Proposed change:

1. Retain executions that end in `FAILED` or `REVERTED` by default. Continue discarding
   `DONE` executions unless a workflow opts in, since successful runs are high volume and
   rarely inspected.
2. Make the default retention window configurable in `medusa-config`.
3. Add a pruning path so the table does not grow without bound.
4. Keep behavior consistent between `workflow-engine-inmemory` and `workflow-engine-redis`.

The main objection to address is storage cost. Retaining every execution on a busy store
would mean significant write volume and table growth, which is presumably why retention is
opt in today. Limiting the default to failed and reverted runs keeps the volume proportional
to the failure rate rather than to total traffic.

**User story**

As a store operator, I want to open a failed workflow execution in the admin dashboard and
see which step failed and which steps were rolled back, so that I can understand why an
order or fulfillment did not complete without reading server logs or filing a support ticket.

As a developer building custom workflows, I want failed executions retained by default, so
that I can verify my compensation logic actually ran without adding my own logging.

**Rough scope**

Large. The data model, the list view, the timeline renderer, and the state handling already
exist, so this does not require building the observability UI. The work is changing the
retention policy in both workflow engines, adding a configuration surface for the default
window, and adding pruning. Suggested decomposition for a later sprint:

1. Add a config option for the default retention policy
2. Retain failed and reverted executions in `workflow-engine-inmemory`
3. Same change in `workflow-engine-redis`
4. Add a pruning job for expired executions
5. Add a state filter to the workflow executions list so failures can be found quickly

**Source**

checked out in this repository. One open question worth confirming during implementation:
the failure rendering code paths exist, but it is unclear whether they have ever been
exercised against real failed execution data.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 15:02:06Z)**_

Honest answer: the runtime-generation version has two problems, but there's a real feature underneath it.

**The premise doesn't quite hold.** There isn't a per-product workflow that might be missing. `complete-cart` handles every purchase, whatever the item. Product-specific variation is already handled by pluggable providers (payment, fulfillment, tax) and shipping options, not by separate workflows. So "the merchant doesn't have a workflow for this item" isn't a state Medusa can be in.

**Generating it at runtime is the wrong place for it.** Checkout moves money, decrements inventory, and creates legal records. Workflows are safe precisely because each step's compensation is written and tested in advance, so a failure unwinds predictably. A generated compensation function is exactly the code you cannot afford to be wrong, and it would run unreviewed, mid-transaction, on a customer's card. Any reviewer will go straight there.

**But the AI angle is genuinely on-brand.** Medusa describes itself as "an AI-native commerce platform," and your own build output advertised an MCP server and Claude Code plugins at `github.com/medusajs/medusa-claude-plugins`. So agent features fit; the question is where they sit safely.

Two reframes that keep the ambition and survive review:

**A. Agent-assisted workflow authoring, at development time.** A developer describes a custom flow in natural language ("subscription box that charges monthly and skips fulfillment on pause"), and an agent scaffolds the `createStep`/`createWorkflow` code, including compensation functions and tests. The developer reviews, edits, and commits it. Same ambition, but the generated code goes through a human and CI before it ever touches a payment. This is squarely what Medusa's Framework half is for.

**B. Agent-assisted diagnosis of failed workflows.** This one pairs directly with your #16. Once failed executions are retained, an agent reads the step tree, the error, and the payload, and explains what broke and what rolled back in plain language, with a suggested fix. The merchant gets "payment captured but inventory reservation failed because variant X had 0 stock in location Y; the payment was voided" instead of a red step in a timeline.

B is the stronger pitch for your backlog. It builds on an issue you've already filed, it's demonstrably impossible today because the data gets deleted, and it needs no code generation at all, which removes the entire safety objection. It also gives your team a coherent two-issue arc: retain the failures, then make them legible.

If you'd rather keep your original framing, the honest version is narrower: let a merchant *configure* which pre-built steps run for unusual products, with an agent suggesting the configuration. Composition of vetted steps, not generation of new ones.

Which direction do you want? I can draft B as your second ambitious issue, or A if you prefer the authoring angle.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Shopify to Medusa migration tools and plugins:

## Official Migration Solutions

Medusa's MCP server includes a migration tool to move store data from Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, or any platform into Medusa using an AI agent. The MCP server provides support for two migration approaches: a Custom approach that pulls data from Shopify's API, where the import is idempotent and resumable, so it can be triggered on a schedule, from an admin page, via a CLI command, or other custom approaches. There's also a CSV approach that transforms your Shopify product export file into the format Medusa's built-in product importer accepts, useful for a fast, one-time cutover when you can't create a Shopify app.

## Plugin Solutions

The medusa-source-shopify plugin is a source plugin that allows users to import products from a Shopify store. It migrates data related to your products on Shopify to Medusa and also registers a scheduled job that runs periodically and ensures your data is synced between Shopify and Medusa.

## What Gets Imported

After starting your Medusa server, it will synchronize with Shopify and import your products, collections, pricing, variants, and attributes. This migration also covers inventory and images.

## Additional Options

There are also community-built alternatives like an upgraded plugin that takes advantage of medusa's batch processing capabilities to sync between the medusa store and shopify for handling large stores, and medusa-source-shopify-json, which allows migration using .JSON files.

## Medusa Analytics Plugins

The Medusa Analytics Plugin is a lightweight analytics extension for the Medusa Admin dashboard that provides store admins with a clear view of sales and product performance using focused KPIs, charts, and tables, all accessible directly within the Medusa Admin panel.

## Key Features

**Metrics and Visualization:**
- The dashboard presents real-time metrics such as revenue, orders, average order value, and refunds on an hourly graph.
- The plugin includes a Date Range Picker with presets like "This Month," "Last Month," "Last 3 Months," and "Custom Range," along with a Tabbed Interface to switch between Orders and Products analytics.

**Home Page/Sales Overview:**
A Sales Overview Page features three main components: a Header that displays key metrics like revenue and customer counts, a Bar Chart that visualizes sales data by quarter, and a Recent Orders Section that lists recent customer orders.

**Advanced Options:**
Store analytics options include a customizable dashboard where you can create your own dashboard with chosen statistics, a date range picker, and more than 15 advanced statistics including funnels, deep insights about promotions, and granular statistics per sales channels.

## Requirements
The plugin requires Medusa v2.11.0 or later due to its dependency on the Caching Module, which was introduced in that version.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 15:23:15Z)**_

That's your fourth issue, and it's the cleanest gap we've found.

**The engine can retry a failed step. Nothing can ask it to.**

```
Engine:     retryStep() and resume() exist in both the module service and orchestrator
Admin API:  8 workflow routes — run, subscribe, steps/success, steps/failure — but no retry, no cancel
Admin UI:   zero references to retry in the entire workflow-executions feature
```

So a capability is implemented at the core and simply has no path to the operator. Same shape as #16: the expensive part is built, the last mile isn't.

And critically, **this one has to be core.** A plugin can't add it, because the admin API route doesn't exist and plugin authors don't get to add routes to `packages/medusa/src/api/admin`. That's what makes it survive the "just use a plugin" objection that killed the Shopify, dashboard, and abandoned-cart ideas.

> **TITLE:** Add the ability to retry a failed workflow step from the admin dashboard
> **LABELS:** `type: feature`, `scope: xl`
>
> **Summary**
> The workflow engine already supports retrying a failed step. `retryStep` exists on the workflow module service and the orchestrator, and the orchestrator also has a `resume` method. None of it is reachable from outside. The admin API exposes routes for running a workflow, subscribing to it, and reporting step success or failure, but nothing for retrying, and the workflow executions page in the dashboard has no retry action. When a workflow fails partway, the only options are to leave it or redo the work by hand, even though the engine could pick it up again. A retry action should be exposed through the admin API and surfaced on the workflow execution detail page.
>
> **User Story**
> As a store manager, I want to retry a workflow step that failed because of a temporary problem, so that I can finish an order without redoing the work manually.
>
> **Rough Scope**
> XL. Requires adding admin API routes for retry, deciding which failure states are safely retryable and which are not, handling permissions and idempotency so a retry cannot double charge or double reserve, and adding the action to the workflow execution detail page. Depends on failed executions being retained first, which is issue #16.
>
> **Source**
> Medusa, workflow engine and admin dashboard workflow executions page.

The safety question is stated in the scope rather than hidden, because "when is a retry safe" is genuinely the hard part and a reviewer will look for whether you noticed. It also honestly declares the dependency on #16.

Want me to create `scope: xl` and ship it? That completes your four: #16, #17, #18, and this.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 16:29:09Z)**_

Good — teaching the method rather than handing you the files is exactly what D5 wants, and it's what you'll be asked to explain later.

## The core technique

Concept location means starting from something in the **problem domain** (a word the user sees) and tracing it to the code that implements it. Four approaches, in rough order of usefulness here:

**1. Vocabulary search.** Start from user-visible text. In this dashboard that means i18next, so UI strings live in translation JSON, not in components. The trick is two hops: find the string in the translation file, get its key, then grep for the key.

```bash
cd ~/medusa/packages/admin/dashboard
ls src/i18n/translations/          # find the English one
grep -n -i "handle" src/i18n/translations/en.json
# then take the key you find, e.g. "products.fields.handle.label"
grep -rn "products.fields.handle" src/
```

That lands you in the component without guessing at file names.

**2. Find the analogous feature.** This is the highest-value move for #10. Some other list page in this dashboard already has a delete row action — you saw `actions.delete` in the products list earlier. Find a working one, read how it's wired, and mirror it. Most of your implementation is then a known-good pattern rather than invention.

```bash
grep -rln "actions.delete" src/routes/ | head
```

**3. Follow the network call.** Open the running app, DevTools → Network, do the thing (or try to), see which endpoint fires. Then grep the API route in `packages/medusa/src/api/`. This is how you find the backend half and learn whether the API already supports what you need.

**4. Follow the URL.** The route map maps URLs to components. You already know `/products/create` and `/customers` from clicking around.

```bash
grep -n "customers" src/dashboard-app/routes/get-route.map.tsx | head
```

## Starting points for each

**#4, product handle** — you're looking for two things, and they may be in different places: where the create form defines its fields and validation, and whether the backend also validates. Forms in this dashboard use react-hook-form with zod schemas, so search for the schema, not just the input. Ask yourself whether "required" belongs on the client, the server, or both — that's a real design question the issue doesn't answer.

**#10, customer delete** — find the customers list table, then find how another list implements a row action menu and a delete confirmation. Also check whether a delete API already exists (the issue says you can delete from the detail page, so the endpoint almost certainly does). That makes this mostly UI work, which is why it's Small.

## What to write down

D5 grades the notes, so record as you go:

- Which search found each file, and which searches failed
- The file path and what it's responsible for
- The call path: component → hook → API route → service
- Where exactly your change goes, and what else touches that code
- Open questions for the issue author

That last one matters for #10 — the issue says "either via a row action menu or by selecting multiple customers and bulk deleting," and those are different amounts of work. Deciding which, and asking the author, is part of the exercise.

## One tooling note

You have `vite-plugin-inspect` running at http://localhost:5173/__inspect/ — it shows the module graph for the dev server, which can help you see what imports what.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-16 16:37:01Z)**_

Yes, meaningfully easier — and D5 specifically asks you to "navigate code dependencies (e.g., function/method calls)," which is exactly what grep is bad at and an IDE is good at.

**What VS Code gives you that the CLI doesn't:**

- **F12 / Cmd+click** — go to definition. Jump from `handle` in the form straight to the schema that declares it.
- **Shift+F12** — find all references. This is the big one: "who else touches this?" is the question grep can't answer reliably, because grep matches strings and this answers with the type system.
- **Cmd+T** — search symbols by name across the whole repo.
- **Option+F12** — peek definition inline, without losing your place.
- **Cmd+Shift+F** — project-wide search, same as grep but with clickable results and file-tree grouping.

For the rest of this investigation, references and go-to-definition will save you real time. Grep already did its job: vocabulary search is where it shines, and it got you from "Handle" on screen to the component in two hops.

**One monorepo gotcha:** open the repo root (`~/medusa`), not the dashboard package. Yarn workspaces symlink `@medusajs/*` into `node_modules`, so with the root open, go-to-definition on a cross-package import lands in real source. Open just the sub-package and it may drop you in a `.d.ts` file instead, which tells you the type but not the logic.

**One caution that matters for your grade:** if you use Cursor, or VS Code with Copilot, **turn the AI features off for this part.** Go-to-definition and find-references are you reading code, which is what D5 wants. An agent answering "where is handle validated?" is the thing the assignment is explicitly trying to prevent, and you'd be handing back work you can't explain.

Also worth keeping open while you read: the running app at :5173 with DevTools. Submit the create-product form with an empty handle and watch the Network tab. That tells you the exact endpoint and whether the request is even sent, which is evidence neither grep nor the IDE can give you.

## Issue #4 — the premise appears to be wrong

Your tooltip catch was right, and it goes further than you thought.

**Client side:** `product-create/constants.ts:64` — `handle: z.string().optional()`

**Server side:** `product-module-service.ts:3238`
```js
if (!productData.handle && productData.title) {
  productData.handle = toHandle(productData.title)
}
```

**And `toHandle` cannot return empty** — it falls back to `product-<random>`.

**And the model is `handle: model.text()`, not `.nullable()`.** Non-null at the database level.

So a product **cannot** be saved without a handle in 2.17.2. The issue says the storefront 404s because of a missing handle, and cites "an actual Medusa issue" — which likely predates this auto-generation, possibly from v1.

**What I did find that looks like a genuine bug:** the model declares `IDX_product_handle_unique` (unique, where `deleted_at IS NULL`), and there is **no dedupe logic anywhere**. Two products titled "Blue Shirt" both generate `blue-shirt`. The second violates the unique constraint. Nothing catches it, so the user likely gets a raw database error rather than a useful message.

I have not proven that last part — it needs an actual test of creating two same-titled products. That's worth doing before you build anything.

**Your options:**

1. **Comment on #4 with what you found**, ask lefecko whether the intent was a required field or a duplicate-handle problem. Most honest, and D5 explicitly asks you to. Costs you a round-trip.
2. **Implement the literal ask** — make handle required client-side. Small and safe, but arguably makes the product worse by removing a working convenience.
3. **Swap to #17 or #18**, your own issues... except D5 forbids implementing your own.

  useTranslation: () => ({

import { CustomerActions } from "./customer-list-table"

const customer = {
  id: "cus_1",
  email: "someone@example.com",
} as any

const openMenu = async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup()
  await user.click(screen.getByRole("button"))
  return user
}

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.clearAllMocks()
  mockCan.mockReturnValue(true)
  mockPrompt.mockResolvedValue(true)
  mockMutateAsync.mockResolvedValue(undefined)
})

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup()
})

describe("CustomerActions", () => {
  it("offers a delete action when the user may delete customers", async () => {
    render(<CustomerActions customer={customer} />)
    await openMenu()

    expect(await screen.findByText("Delete")).toBeTruthy()
  })

  it("hides the delete action when the user may not delete customers", async () => {
    // Only "update" is permitted, so the menu should still open for Edit but
    // must not offer Delete.
    mockCan.mockImplementation((_resource, action) => action === "update")

    render(<CustomerActions customer={customer} />)
    await openMenu()

    expect(await screen.findByText("Edit")).toBeTruthy()
    expect(screen.queryByText("Delete")).toBeNull()
  })

  it("deletes the customer once the prompt is confirmed", async () => {
    render(<CustomerActions customer={customer} />)
    const user = await openMenu()

    await user.click(await screen.findByText("Delete"))

    await waitFor(() => expect(mockMutateAsync).toHaveBeenCalled())
    expect(mockPrompt).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ verificationText: customer.email })
    )
  })

  it("does not delete the customer when the prompt is cancelled", async () => {
    mockPrompt.mockResolvedValue(false)

    render(<CustomerActions customer={customer} />)
    const user = await openMenu()

    await user.click(await screen.findByText("Delete"))

    await waitFor(() => expect(mockPrompt).toHaveBeenCalled())
    expect(mockMutateAsync).not.toHaveBeenCalled()
  })
})

2. `handleDelete` is lifted from `customer-general-section.tsx` — same `usePrompt` with type-to-confirm on the customer's email, same `useDeleteCustomer(customer.id).mutateAsync`, same toasts. **One deliberate difference:** the detail page calls `navigate("/customers")` afterward; the list version drops that, since you're already there.
3. The component is now exported so the test can render the menu alone instead of mounting the whole table with react-query and a router.
4. Four tests: delete appears with permission, is absent without it, runs the mutation on confirm, and does nothing on cancel.

What: Adds a live character counter below the product description field, shown while creating or editing a product, so users can track description length as they type.

Why: The description field had no way to see how long the text was. This will assist store managers with making sure their descriptions aren't too lengthy or short.

Each gets a Form.Hint right after the textarea. 
field.value comes from react-hook-form's Controller, which already re-renders on every keystroke, so the count is live with no extra state. The two forms don't share a component, and the addition is one line each, so it's implemented inline in both rather than introducing a new shared component for it.

Testing: product-create-general-section.spec.tsx (4 tests) and edit-product-form.spec.tsx (3 tests) both cover: starts at "0 characters", updates live while typing, and uses the singular "1 character" correctly. The edit-form suite exercises the real route-level component (router, extension context, and query client wired up), not just the isolated field, since that form pulls in several route-level dependencies the create-form section doesn't.

cat > __tests__/constants.spec.ts <<'EOF'
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest"

import { ProductCreateSchema } from "../constants"

// The schema has several other required fields, so parsing a bare object will
// always produce errors. These tests only care about whether "handle" is one
// of them, so they look at the issues for that path rather than at whether the
// whole parse succeeded.
const handleIssues = (input: Record<string, unknown>) => {
  const result = ProductCreateSchema.safeParse(input)

  if (result.success) {
    return []
  }

  return result.error.issues.filter((issue) => issue.path[0] === "handle")
}

describe("ProductCreateSchema", () => {
  it("rejects a product with no handle", () => {
    expect(handleIssues({ title: "Winter jacket" })).not.toHaveLength(0)
  })

  it("rejects a product with an empty handle", () => {
    expect(
      handleIssues({ title: "Winter jacket", handle: "" })
    ).not.toHaveLength(0)
  })

  it("accepts a product with a handle", () => {
    expect(
      handleIssues({ title: "Winter jacket", handle: "winter-jacket" })
    ).toHaveLength(0)
  })

  it("still requires a title", () => {
    const result = ProductCreateSchema.safeParse({ handle: "winter-jacket" })

    expect(result.success).toBe(false)

    if (!result.success) {
      const titleIssues = result.error.issues.filter(
        (issue) => issue.path[0] === "title"
      )
      expect(titleIssues).not.toHaveLength(0)
    }
  })
})
EOF

Closes #4

Summary

What: Makes the handle field required on the product create form, and drops the "optional" marker from its label.

Why: The issue is that products can be created without a handle and then 404 on the storefront. Requiring it up front means the URL a product gets is one the person creating it actually chose.

How: ProductCreateSchema in product-create/constants.ts had handle as z.string().optional(), so it's now z.string().min(1), matching how title is already declared right above it. One thing I want to flag, because it changes what this PR actually does. While tracing where the handle gets set I found that the server already fills one in: product-module-service.ts does `if (!productData.handle && productData.title) productData.handle = toHandle(productData.title)`, and toHandle falls back to a random `product-xxxxxx` string if the title reduces to nothing. The column is model.text() with no .nullable(), so as far as I can tell a product can't currently be saved with an empty handle on 2.17.2. The 404 in the issue may predate that auto-generation.

So this is a UX change rather than a data integrity fix: it makes you pick the handle instead of silently getting a generated one. I still think that's worth doing, since a generated handle can be something you didn't expect, but I didn't want to describe it as fixing missing handles when it isn't.

Separately, product.handle has a unique index (IDX_product_handle_unique) and I couldn't find any dedupe logic, so two products with the same title both generate the same handle and the second should hit a constraint error. I haven't tested that and it's out of scope here, but it seems worth its own issue.

## What the change actually is

Two edits, 2 lines added, 5 removed.

**1. `constants.ts:64`** — the zod schema for the create form:
```diff
-    handle: z.string().optional(),
+    handle: z.string().min(1),
```
`.optional()` means the key can be absent entirely. `.min(1)` means it must be a string of at least one character, so both a missing key and `""` now fail validation. I matched `title: z.string().min(1)` two lines above rather than inventing a different style or a custom error message — the form will use zod's default message, the same way title does.

**2. `product-create-general-section.tsx:64`** — removed the `optional` prop from the field's `Form.Label`. Without this the label would still say "optional" while the schema rejected an empty value. That's a UI/validation mismatch, not a cosmetic detail.

Nothing else. No backend change, no new dependency.

## How we know it works

Four independent checks:

**Typecheck passes** — `yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard typecheck`, exit 0. The schema type is inferred via `z.infer`, so if `.min(1)` had broken the derived `ProductCreateSchemaType`, this would fail.

**The tests fail without the fix.** This is the one that actually matters. I put `.optional()` back and reran:
```
Tests  2 failed | 2 passed (4)
 FAIL  rejects a product with no handle
 FAIL  rejects a product with an empty handle
```
Then restored it and all 4 passed. So the tests are tied to the behavior rather than passing vacuously.

**Nothing else broke** — full dashboard suite, 13 files / 93 tests, exit 0. That includes njpiombino's `product-create-general-section.spec.tsx`, which renders this exact component, so their test would have caught it if removing `optional` broke the label.

**What is *not* verified: I never clicked it in a browser.** For #10 you loaded the page and confirmed Delete worked. For this one nobody has opened the create-product form and tried submitting without a handle. The tests cover the schema, not the rendered form's error display or submit-button state.

That's a real gap, and it's the thing I'd check before letting this merge — `PRODUCT_CREATE_FORM_DEFAULTS` sets `handle: ""`, so the form now starts in an invalid state, and I haven't seen how that presents.

You can check in about a minute: **http://localhost:5173/products/create**, fill in a title, clear the handle, try to continue. You should be blocked with an error on the handle field, and the label shouldn't say optional.

Tell me whether to close #21 while you look.

import { useTranslation } from "react-i18next"
import { RouteFocusModal } from "../../../components/modals"
import { useRegions } from "../../../hooks/api"
import { usePricePreferences } from "../../../hooks/api/price-preferences"
import { useSalesChannel } from "../../../hooks/api/sales-channels"
import { useStore } from "../../../hooks/api/store"
import { ProductCreateForm } from "./components/product-create-form/product-create-form"

export const ProductCreate = () => {
  const { t } = useTranslation()

  const {
    store,
    isPending: isStorePending,
    isError: isStoreError,
    error: storeError,
  } = useStore({
    fields: "+default_sales_channel",
  })

  const {
    sales_channel,
    isPending: isSalesChannelPending,
    isError: isSalesChannelError,
    error: salesChannelError,
  } = useSalesChannel(store?.default_sales_channel_id!, {
    enabled: !!store?.default_sales_channel_id,
  })

  const {
    regions,
    isPending: isRegionsPending,
    isError: isRegionsError,
    error: regionsError,
  } = useRegions({ limit: 9999 })

  const {
    price_preferences,
    isPending: isPricePreferencesPending,
    isError: isPricePreferencesError,
    error: pricePreferencesError,
  } = usePricePreferences({
    limit: 9999,
  })

  const ready =
    !!store &&
    !isStorePending &&
    !!regions &&
    !isRegionsPending &&
    !!sales_channel &&
    !isSalesChannelPending &&
    !!price_preferences &&
    !isPricePreferencesPending

  if (isStoreError) {
    throw storeError
  }

  if (isRegionsError) {
    throw regionsError
  }

  if (isSalesChannelError) {
    throw salesChannelError
  }

  if (isPricePreferencesError) {
    throw pricePreferencesError
  }

  return (
    <RouteFocusModal>
      <RouteFocusModal.Title asChild>
        <span className="sr-only">{t("products.create.title")}</span>
      </RouteFocusModal.Title>
      <RouteFocusModal.Description asChild>
        <span className="sr-only">{t("products.create.description")}</span>
      </RouteFocusModal.Description>
      {ready && (
        <ProductCreateForm
          defaultChannel={sales_channel}
          store={store}
          pricePreferences={price_preferences}
          regions={regions}
        />
      )}
    </RouteFocusModal>
  )
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-17 03:10:46Z)**_

Found the actual cause, and it's bigger than your issue.

```
zod                   4.2.0
@hookform/resolvers   3.4.2      <- built for zod 3
react-hook-form       7.49.1
```

`useExtendableForm` (`dashboard-app/forms/hooks.ts:103`) wires `resolver: zodResolver(schema)`. **Resolvers v3 doesn't understand zod 4's error API**, so instead of converting the `ZodError` into form state, it lets it throw. My test caught it throwing with both errors intact:

```json
{ "path": ["title"],  "message": "Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters" }
{ "path": ["handle"], "message": "Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters" }
```

The validation works perfectly. The errors just never reach `formState.errors`, so no field can ever display one.

**This is pre-existing and repo-wide, not caused by my change.** It's why `title` has no `Form.ErrorMessage` and why nobody noticed — messages have never rendered in any form using this hook. It also explains the behavior you saw exactly: `form.trigger()` throws, `onNext` never advances, and you get a silent block.

Same family as the `@medusajs/icons` React 19/18 problem: a dependency major-version mismatch that the type system doesn't catch.

What this means for #21:

- The schema change is **correct** — a blank handle is now genuinely rejected, which is what the issue asked for.
- The user experience is **still poor**, and my `Form.ErrorMessage` addition can't fix it while the resolver is broken.
- Fixing the resolver means upgrading `@hookform/resolvers` to v5, which touches every form in the dashboard. Way outside #4.

Your options:

1. **Ship #21 with the schema change**, drop my `Form.ErrorMessage` addition (it does nothing today), and note the resolver bug in the description plus a new issue. Honest and scoped.
2. **Keep `Form.ErrorMessage`** anyway, since it's correct and will start working once the resolver is fixed.
3. **Close #21** until the resolver is sorted, on the grounds that requiring a field with no error message is a worse experience than not requiring it.

I'd go with 1 or 2 — the change does what the issue asked, and the silent-failure problem predates it. But 3 is defensible and you're the one who has to argue it.

Which? And separately: the tooltip still needs updating, since it now contradicts the requirement.

Closes #4

Summary

What: Makes the handle field required when creating a product, and removes the bit of the tooltip that said a handle would be generated for you.

Why: Products could be saved without a handle, and the handle is what the storefront uses to find the product.

How: In product-create/constants.ts the schema had handle as z.string().optional(), so it's now z.string().min(1), same as title right above it. The label had an "optional" prop that had to come off too, and the tooltip said "If not specified, the handle will be generated from the product title", which isn't true anymore, so that sentence is gone.

Testing: 4 tests in product-create/__tests__/constants.spec.ts: missing handle, empty handle, valid handle, and title still required.

Run them with: yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard test constants

Full suite passes (13 files, 93 tests) and typecheck is clean. I also put the old .optional() back for a second and confirmed two of the tests fail without the change.

Two things I found while doing this

1. The server already generates a handle if you don't give it one. product-module-service.ts does `if (!productData.handle && productData.title) productData.handle = toHandle(productData.title)`, and toHandle falls back to a random "product-xxxxxx" if the title has nothing usable in it. The column is also not nullable. So on 2.17.2 I don't think you can actually end up with an empty handle, and the 404 in the issue probably predates that. This PR still makes you pick the handle instead of getting a generated one, which I think is worth having, but it's a UX change more than a bug fix and I didn't want to claim otherwise.

2. You won't see an error message when you leave the handle blank. The form just refuses to continue. That's not something this PR can fix. The dashboard has @hookform/resolvers 3.4.2 with zod 4.2.0, and that version of the resolver doesn't understand zod 4's errors, so instead of putting them in form state it throws. I confirmed it by running the validation directly and the handle error is there with a message, it just never reaches the form. This affects every form in the dashboard: 116 files use zodResolver and 104 render <Form.ErrorMessage />, and none of them can show anything right now. Title has the same problem and always has.

I left the error message component out of this PR since it wouldn't do anything today. Happy to add it once the resolver is sorted. I'm opening a separate issue for that.
